text: Hoi An might be famous for its lanterns, but the food here is arguably even better. Over three days in the Old Town, we set ourselves a challenge: try every local dish we could find. From city-exclusive noodle soups and street food snails that required a local’s lesson, to tabletop charcoal grills and $1 desserts this is everything we ate in Hoi An. And we’re starting with one of Vietnam’s most famous dishes. Our first stop was Pho Xua. Pho is probably the most famous Vietnamese dish in the world. The broth is simmered for hours with star anise, cinnamon, and cloves. It arrives steaming hot, loaded with thin slices of beef, soft rice noodles, and fresh herbs. The broth is rich yet surprisingly light At 70,000 VND, about $3, it’s a steal. But because we were in Hoi An… there was another noodle dish we absolutely had to try. And it’s something you rarely find anywhere else. That dish is cao lầu. Cao lầu actually originated here in Hoi An centuries ago when the town was a major trading port. The noodles are thicker and chewier than pho. They’re topped with slices of pork, crispy crackers, and fresh herbs. Our bowl cost 60,000 VND. The textures are what make this dish special: chewy noodles, crunchy toppings, and fragrant herbs. It’s an absolute local staple. But after two noodle dishes… we needed something refreshing. The afternoon heat in Hoi An can be intense. Luckily, fresh coconuts are everywhere. We stopped at a small street stall where she chopped open the coconut right in front of us And it only cost 20,000 VND that's less than a dollar. But Hoi An also has a dessert locals love in the afternoon. Later we found a small dessert stall called Chè Hai Chị Em. They specialize in chè, often translated as Vietnamese sweet soup. It usually includes beans, jelly, coconut milk, and crushed ice. It was creamy, sweet, and really comforting in the heat. We sat outside on small chairs watching bikes pass by and locals stopping for dessert. Next up is a snack we’ve come to absolutely love. Bánh mì Its Vietnam’s take on a sandwich, influenced by French baguettes but filled with Vietnamese flavors usually a mix of meats, pickled vegetables, herbs, chili, and sauce. Hoi An’s bread stays light and crisp, and the fillings stay balanced instead of overpowering. What’s nice is that bánh mì is everywhere in Hoi An. Many cafés and night market stalls offer their own versions, all of them were honestly delicious. But as the sun started setting the entire food scene in Hoi An completely changed. And we ended up trying one of the strangest street foods of the trip. One of the most interesting things we saw everywhere… was snails served with herbs and rice paper. When the food arrived, we honestly had no idea how to eat it. The table suddenly filled with herbs, rice paper, grilled pork, and snails. So we ended up watching the locals next to us. They wrapped everything together like a fresh spring roll. Herbs. Pork. Snails. All in one bite. Once we tried it the flavors actually made perfect sense. It was delicious. But we still had a big dinner planned. And Hoi An has a dish locals are incredibly proud of. For dinner we went to Cơm Gà Giếng Đình. This place was packed. Hoi An is famous for chicken rice. The rice is cooked in chicken broth and turmeric, giving it its bright yellow color. Our chicken rice cost 40,000 VND, and we also ordered a half chicken platter for 250,000 VND. The staff gave us a quick lesson on how to eat like a local, mixing the savory chicken and fragrant rice with fresh herbs, sauces, and crunchy vegetables for the perfect bite It became one of our favorite dishes during our trip. But the most fun meal of the night was still ahead. Later we found a small family-run restaurant called BBQ Nướng Khói. Instead of cooking in the kitchen they brought out a clay pot filled with charcoal and placed a grill right on our table. We went all out with the menu, ordering everything from spicy pork ribs to beef-wrapped mushrooms and grilled oysters It was a fun, interactive experience, with the charcoal giving everything a perfect smoky finish But before ending the night… we still had room for one last street snack. While walking through the night market, we spotted a stall making banana pancakes. The vendor poured batter onto a hot griddle, topped it with sliced bananas, and finished it with a generous drizzle of chocolate syrup. At only 10,000 VND (about 40 cents), it was the perfect late-night snack But before heading back to the hotel, we made one final stop. We passed by a bakery with trays of fresh croissants still on display. Vietnam actually has a strong baking culture because of its French colonial history. With everything from croissants to soft sponge cakes starting at just $1–$2, these bakeries are a must-visit. We grabbed some pastries for the next morning, which we ended up enjoying at the hotel with our Vietnamese coffee If you enjoyed this Hoi An food tour, like the video and follow for more travel and food guides. And let us know which dish you’d want to try first.
